bib.title: Sparse Kernel Machines (Chapter 7 of Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning)
bib.venue: Springer, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, ch. 7, pp. 325-358

question: How can kernel methods be made to give sparse solutions so predictions depend on only a subset of training points, and what do the SVM and the RVM each offer?
contributions: Maximum margin classifier, soft-margin SVM, nu-SVM, SVM regression and their dual QPs (Sec 7.1)
Link between SVM hinge loss and logistic regression, multiclass and one-class SVM variants
Relevance vector machine as ARD Bayesian sparse kernel model, with a fast sequential training algorithm (Sec 7.2)

limits: SVM outputs are decisions, not posterior probabilities; Platt scaling is a post-hoc fix and can approximate posteriors poorly (p.336).
SVM was formulated for two classes; multiclass extension 'remains an open issue' and one-versus-the-rest is used in spite of its ad-hoc formulation (p.339).
C, nu and epsilon must be set by cross-validation (p.345); the chapter picks them by hand in its figures.
RVM training optimizes a nonconvex function, can be slower than SVM, needs M x M inversion O(M^3) (p.349).
RVM predictive variance shrinks away from the data when basis functions sit on data points (p.348), unlike Gaussian processes.
PAC bounds are very conservative and have found few if any practical applications (p.345).

No quantitative benchmark: all figures are small synthetic 2-D illustrations; speed and sparsity claims are cited from Tipping (2001), not shown. Dated: 2006 text, no coverage of large-scale linear SVMs, deep kernels or later solvers.
practices: Use the averaged formula (Eq 7.18 / 7.37) over support vectors (over those with 0<a_n<C in the soft case) to compute b, for numerical stability (pp.330, 334).
Choose C (or nu, epsilon) by cross-validation (p.343, p.345).
Fit Platt's sigmoid on data independent of the SVM training set (p.336).
For multiclass SVMs, one-versus-the-rest is the most widely used approach despite its limits (p.339).
Prefer a monotonically decreasing loss (hinge or logistic) over squared error when the goal is low misclassification rate (p.338).
Average the b estimates over all valid points in SVM regression (p.343).
For RVM, use the sequential sparse Bayesian learning algorithm (p.352-353), which adds, re-estimates or removes one basis function at a time.

code.where: pp.352-353, Sequential Sparse Bayesian Learning Algorithm
code.snippet: 1 init beta (regression); 2 start with one basis phi_1, alpha_1 by (7.101), others alpha=inf; 3 compute Sigma, m, q_i, s_i for all; 4 pick candidate phi_i; 5 if q_i^2>s_i and alpha_i<inf: update alpha_i = s_i^2/(q_i^2-s_i); 6 if q_i^2>s_i and alpha_i=inf: add phi_i; 7 if q_i^2<=s_i and alpha_i<inf: remove phi_i, alpha_i=inf; 8 update beta (regression); 9 stop if converged else go to 3
alpha_i_new = gamma_i / m_i^2 ; (beta_new)^-1 = ||t - Phi m||^2 / (N - sum_i gamma_i) ; gamma_i = 1 - alpha_i Sigma_ii

problems: Equations are garbled in the text extraction (superscripts, inverses, tildes, hats lost); e.g. Eq 7.113 and 7.119 print without visible inverse markers, so (7.119) 'C = B + ΦAΦT' as extracted cannot be checked against the printed book. Treat these as extraction faults, not book errors, unless confirmed in the PDF.
Inconsistency in the chapter: Eq 7.118 is written ln p(t|alpha, beta) for the classification RVM, which has no beta; likely a carry-over from the regression form (7.85).
Mild inconsistency: Sec 7.1.1 calls the nu-SVM 'ν replaces C' with a_n <= 1/N while the regression nu-SVM (7.71-7.72) keeps C with a_n <= C/N.
Sec 7.1.1 says the dual 'minimize[s] (7.32)' with respect to a, whereas Eq 7.10 and the text before say 'maximize'.
Intro says RVM gives 'typically much sparser solutions'; Sec 7.2 says 'an order of magnitude'; both are citations of Tipping 2001, no table in the chapter.
Fig 7.4 nu value and Fig 7.8 nu and C values are not given in text. Exercises (7.1-7.19) are present but not recorded as results.
